papers.title: Clinical Hypnosis for Chronic Non-Cancer Pain: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Chronic non-cancer pain requires multimodal management, and clinical hypnosis has been examined as a complementary intervention. This PRISMA ScR scoping review mapped the extent and characteristics of the evidence base, intervention features, and research gaps for clinical hypnosis in chronic non-cancer pain. We included 48 intervention studies involving 3,166 participants, encompassing randomized controlled trials and other study designs. Hypnosis was applied to nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic, and mixed pain presentations using diverse techniques and delivery formats. Outcomes most frequently included pain intensity and pain related distress, with additional measures of coping, sleep, and daily functioning. The mapped literature commonly involved small samples, frequent use of passive comparators, limited demographic reporting and diversity, and variable intervention reporting. This review extends prior syntheses by detailing how clinical hypnosis has been operationalized for chronic non-cancer pain and by identifying methodological and reporting gaps to guide future research.

papers.title: Quantitative Analysis of Electroencephalography in Hypnosis: A Neurophysiological Approach.
papers.abstract: Hypnosis is a unique state of consciousness marked by heightened response to suggestions, focused attention, and altered cognitive control. This article explores the neural connections involved in hypnosis through electroencephalography (EEG) studies, examining brain changes during hypnosis and their relationship to hypnotic depth and susceptibility. Theta waves, linked to hypnotic depth, are stronger in highly hypnotizable individuals, while gamma waves are associated with focus, suggestion acceptance, and emotional responses. Hypnosis also induces frequency-dependent reorganization of large-scale brain connectivity, particularly in frontal-parietal and attentional networks, enhancing subjective experiences and responsiveness. EEG patterns reveal more dynamic neural activity during hypnosis, which cannot be captured by linear metrics alone. Hemispheric analysis shows greater left-hemisphere activity in highly hypnotizable individuals, particularly in emotionally and verbally mediated tasks, challenging the right-hemisphere dominance model. Event related potential (ERP) findings show that hypnosis affects information processing at both pre-attentional and cognitive levels. These insights contribute to understanding hypnosis' impact on the brain and its potential for personalized therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Comment on Martyn-Nemeth et al. Sleep Optimization to Improve Glycemic Targets in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Controlled Parallel Intervention Trial.
Modification of locomotion-respiration coupling in patients with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome.
papers.abstract: Locomotion is a complex motor task integrating sensory-motor and cognitive inputs through central pattern generator control. Locomotion-respiration coupling (LRC), defined as the synchronization between gait and breathing events, has been described during running and walking. Patients with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) exhibit altered gait patterns during wakefulness, which appear to be partially independent of nocturnal symptomatic treatment. While intermittent hypoxia may induce long-term ("fixed") central nervous system alterations, OSAS patients also display "reversible" adaptive mechanisms during wakefulness aimed at preventing upper airway (UA) collapse, involving changes in respiratory control and posture. Whether these adaptive mechanisms affect LRC and contribute to gait alterations remains unknown. Ten awake patients with controlled OSAS treated with a mandibular advancement device (MAD) and ten matched healthy controls performed a one-minute walking trial on an instrumented treadmill with motion capture. Ventilation was assessed via thoracic expansion, and spatiotemporal gait parameters were extracted from kinematic and force platform data. LRC was quantified using phase-locking values (PLV) between ventilatory events and sagittal-plane joint kinematics. OSAS patients were assessed both with and without their MAD. Compared with controls, OSAS patients exhibited a longer double-stance phase and a shorter swing phase. Expiratory events occurred preferentially during double stance in OSAS patients, whereas controls showed a higher occurrence during swing. PLV analysis revealed increased synchronization between inspiratory events and hip and knee motion, as well as between expiratory events and trunk and hip motion in OSAS patients. These significative differences were no longer observed when patients wore their MAD. Logistic regression demonstrated that PLV metrics of inspiratory-hip and expiratory-trunk coupling effectively discriminated OSAS patients from controls, but not when UA stabilization was applied. Awake patients with controlled OSAS exhibit altered gait patterns characterized by increased locomotion-respiration coupling. This heightened synchronization likely reflects adaptive, reversible strategies aimed at limiting UA collapsibility during wakefulness rather than fixed hypoxia-related impairments alone. LRC may represent a functional marker of daytime motor alterations in OSAS and a potential target for interventions addressing UA mechanics beyond nocturnal treatment.

papers.title: Type 1 diabetes in the youngest: from distinct needs to new frontiers in care.
papers.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) in very young children poses unique clinical and psychosocial challenges due to distinct physiological, developmental, and behavioural characteristics of this age group. Advances in diabetes technology, particularly hybrid closed-loop (HCL) systems, are transforming T1D management in young children by integrating continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with automated insulin delivery (AID). Evidence from randomized controlled trials and real-world studies consistently demonstrates that HCL systems improve time in range, lower HbA1c, and reduce glycaemic variability without increasing the risk of severe hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis. Benefits are especially evident overnight, when glycaemic control is more stable, although daytime management remains more complex, due to unpredictable behaviours typical of preschoolers and marked circadian variability in insulin needs. Accordingly, the use of HCL fail to decrease hypoglycaemia in this population. Additional strategies, such as insulin dilution, may facilitate safer delivery of small doses, reducing the risk of nocturnal hypoglycaemia and improving time in range (TIR). Beyond metabolic outcomes, HCL systems substantially improve quality of life for both children and caregivers, reducing fear of hypoglycaemia, easing parental burden, and improving sleep and emotional well-being. Overall, current evidence supports HCL as a safe and effective therapeutic option for very young children with T1D, offering significant metabolic and psychosocial benefits, without completely eliminating the risk of hypoglycaemia. These findings highlight the need for further refinement of age-specific algorithms capable of addressing the unique physiological variability of this population.

papers.title: A comparison of clinical and procedural outcomes of transforaminal versus parasagittal interlaminar epidural steroid injections for radicular pain secondary to lumbar disc herniation.
papers.abstract: This study aims to compare the clinical and procedural outcomes of transforaminal epidural steroid injections (TFESIs) and parasagittal interlaminar epidural steroid injections (P-ILESIs) in patients with unilateral radicular pain secondary to lumbar disc herniation (LDH). Between January 2024 and June 2025, a total of 162 patients with unilateral radicular pain caused by single-level LDH were included in this retrospective, observational cohort study. The patients were divided into the two groups based on the technique as the TFESI group (n = 82) and the P-ILESI group (n = 80). Pain, disability, sleep quality, and health-related quality of life were assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Short Form-12 (SF-12), respectively at baseline, one month, and six months. Fluoroscopy time and cumulative radiation dose were also recorded. Of the patients, 120 were male and 42 were female with a median age of 47 (range 22 to 65) years. Both techniques significantly improved pain, disability, sleep quality, and quality of life at one and six months (p < 0.001). The reduction in NRS from baseline was greater with TFESI at one month (p = 0.008), but not at six months (p = 0.545). The ODI scores were lower with TFESI at one month, although the magnitude of improvement from baseline did not significantly differ and no difference was observed at six months. Quality of life outcomes were comparable between the groups. The P-ILESI required longer fluoroscopy time and higher radiation exposure than TFESI (p < 0.001 for both). No major complications occurred, and minor adverse events were infrequent and comparable between the groups (p = 0.764). Both TFESI and P-ILESI appear to be effective and safe approaches for the treatment of radicular pain associated with LDH. The choice of epidural approach should be individualized according to clinical and anatomical considerations, as well as operator experience.

papers.title: EEG-Based Characterization of Cortical Dynamics during Graded Resistance Exercise.
papers.abstract: Understanding how brain activity varies during voluntary movement under different resistance conditions may provide insights into neural responses associated with physical demands and inform the development of neurorehabilitation strategies. In this study, we investigated changes in neural activity associated with increasing resistance levels during unilateral bicep curl movement. Ten healthy participants performed bicep curls under five resistance conditions while their cortical activity was recorded using electroencephalography (EEG). Movement-related cortical potentials (MRCPs), power spectral density (PSD) topographies, nonparametric spatiotemporal cluster-based permutation tests and linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were used to characterize EEG differences across resistance conditions. Differences in MR-CPs and frequency-specific power spectral density (PSD) patterns were observed across resistance conditions, with significant spatiotemporal clusters identified during pre-movement, peak contraction, and movement execution phases. A Triplet Temporal Convolutional Network (TTCN) was also employed to learn latent representations from these EEG signals, and its discriminative capability was evaluated using a k-nearest neighbors (KNN) classifier. The learned embeddings showed separation between the resistance conditions, with classification errors occurring primarily between neighboring conditions. Using a within subject leave-one-trial-out (LOTO) evaluation strategy, the TTCN-KNN framework achieved accuracy of 97.2%. Furthermore, subject-independent evaluation were conducted using a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) approach, achieving a maximum accuracy of 93.0%. These findings suggest that EEG signals contain discriminative information for distinguishing the resistance conditions in both within-subject and subject-independent settings, providing preliminary in sights for future EEG-based monitoring of motor effort and adaptive brain-machine interface applications.

papers.title: Modic changes, chronic low back pain, and lifestyle and mental health factors: a cross-sectional analysis of a cohort study.
papers.abstract: Modic changes (MC) are vertebral endplate and adjacent bone marrow MRI findings that have been associated with chronic low back pain (CLBP), although their clinical relevance remains debated. This study examined whether MC presence and extent are associated with CLBP status, pain intensity, and disability, and whether lifestyle or mental health factors moderate the MC-pain relationship. This exploratory cross-sectional sub-study included 239 adults: 135 with CLBP and 104 controls without. Lumbar MRI scans were evaluated for MC presence, type, craniocaudal extent of vertebral body involvement, and transverse extent of endplate involvement. Firth penalized logistic regression examined associations of MC presence, type and extent with CLBP status. Linear regression models examined associations between aggregated MC count and vertebral body and endplate extent with low back pain intensity and disability within CLBP and control groups. Moderation analyses tested whether sleep disturbance, physical activity, anxiety, depression, or pain catastrophizing modified the association between MC count and low back pain intensity among individuals with CLBP. All models were adjusted for age, sex, smoking, and body mass index. Any MC were associated with higher odds of CLBP (OR 2.50, 95% CI 1.45-4.30; p = 0.001), with similar associations for Type 1 and Type 2 MC. Greater vertebral body involvement showed a graded association with CLBP, with > 50% vertebral body involvement associated with the highest odds (OR 4.88, 95% CI 1.14-20.92; p = 0.033). Among individuals with CLBP, aggregated MC count (β = 0.30, 95% CI 0.05-0.55; p = 0.019) and vertebral body extent (β = 0.11, 95% CI 0.01-0.21; p = 0.039) were associated with higher pain intensity, but not disability. Endplate extent was not associated with pain or disability. None of the examined lifestyle or psychological factors significantly moderated the MC-pain association. This exploratory analysis revealed that MC, particularly those with greater vertebral body involvement, were associated with CLBP status and low back pain intensity. Lifestyle and psychological factors were related to pain severity but did not significantly modify the MC-pain relationship. These findings suggest that MC extent may be a clinically relevant imaging characteristic, although longitudinal studies are needed to clarify causality and prognostic significance.

papers.title: Vibrational dynamics of TODD-graphene nanosheets via molecular dynamics simulations and machine-learning surrogate models: implications for adaptive nanomechanical devices.
papers.abstract: TODD-Graphene (TODD-G), a porous two-dimensional carbon allotrope composed of interconnected 3-8-10-12 carbon rings, has recently emerged as a promising candidate for nanoelectromechanical and adaptive nanodevice applications due to its metallic conductivity, mechanical compliance, and topologically engineered phonon structure. In this work, the vibrational dynamics of TODD-G nanosheets were systematically investigated to establish structure-property relationships governing resonant behavior under varying geometric, thermal, mechanical, and defect conditions. Fundamental frequencies were found to span 2.93-13.28 THz and follow the classical f ∝ L - 2 scaling relation. Increasing temperature from 1 to 1000 K reduced resonance frequencies by up to 22% because of thermal expansion and anharmonic phonon interactions, while tensile strain up to 10% enhanced frequencies by more than 50%, yielding gauge factors of 5.3-5.7 that exceed those of graphene. Vacancy defects significantly degraded quality factors and resonance stability, whereas multilayer stacking improved energy retention despite modest frequency reduction. Boundary conditions strongly altered modal spectra, with clamped-clamped configurations producing the highest frequencies and quality factors. Phonon density-of-states analysis revealed distinct acoustic, mixed, and optical vibrational regimes with a maximum phonon cutoff frequency of 56.5 THz. To accelerate device-level optimization, machine-learning surrogate models were developed for predicting resonance frequency and quality factor across the multidimensional design space. Gradient-boosting models achieved excellent predictive accuracy ( R 2 = 0.98 for frequency and R 2 = 0.972 for quality factor), demonstrating that thermal activation and vacancy concentration dominate vibrational dissipation mechanisms. The combined molecular dynamics and machine-learning framework establishes TODD-G as a promising platform for tunable nanoresonators, strain sensors, RF filters, vibration energy harvesters, and cryogenic nanomechanical systems. Atomic-scale simulations were performed using classical molecular dynamics within the large-scale atomic/molecular massively parallel simulator (LAMMPS) package. Interatomic interactions were described using the adaptive intermolecular reactive empirical bond order (AIREBO) potential with activated Lennard-Jones and torsional terms, while multilayer van der Waals interactions employed a 12-6 Lennard-Jones potential. Structural relaxation was conducted using conjugate-gradient energy minimization. Thermal equilibration employed the Nosé-Hoover thermostat within the canonical (NVT) ensemble, followed by microcanonical (NVE) simulations for vibrational analysis using a timestep of 0.5 fs. Vibrational properties were extracted using impulse-response analysis, velocity autocorrelation functions, harmonic forcing, fast Fourier transform (FFT) spectral analysis, and phonon density-of-states calculations. Simulations systematically examined the effects of nanosheet size, temperature (1-1000 K), tensile strain (0-10%), vacancy-defect concentration (0.5-5%), multilayer stacking (1-5 layers), and boundary conditions (free-free, clamped-free, simply supported, and clamped-clamped). Machine-learning surrogate models including linear regression, support-vector regression with radial-basis-function kernels, random forest regression, and gradient-boosting regression were trained using an 80/20 train-test split and five-fold cross-validation to predict resonance frequency and quality factor across the multidimensional parameter space.

papers.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Sequencing Identifies Altered Expression of Circadian Rhythm-Related Genes Pomc and Bmp4 in Post-Stroke Depression.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke depression (PSD) is a serious complication that significantly hinders stroke patients' recovery and quality of life. Uncovering the molecular changes that drive PSD is vital for understanding how depression develops following a stroke. In this study, we established a reproducible PSD model using minimally invasive photochemical-induced focal cortical lesion. Transcriptomic sequencing demonstrated that dysregulation of circadian entrainment genes is a central pathway in the development of post-stroke depressive-like behaviors. Protein-protein interaction network analysis of these circadian rhythm-related genes identified six hub genes. Four of these, including Pomc and Bmp4, exhibited expression patterns consistent with experimental validation. Integrated single-cell transcriptomic analysis further pinpointed cell-type-specific expression abnormalities of Pomc in endothelial cells and Bmp4 in oligodendrocytes. Subsequently, in silico perturbation analysis further indicated that their shared underlying regulatory mechanisms involve cell adhesion and extracellular matrix interaction. Collectively, using transcriptomic and single-cell sequencing in a PSD model, this study revealed altered expression patterns of circadian rhythm-related genes, providing potential targets for further investigation into the pathogenesis of PSD.

papers.title: Circadian regulation of the S1PR1-P2X7 signalling axis in obesity-associated metabolic inflammation: molecular crosstalk and therapeutic perspectives.
papers.abstract: Obesity is a chronic, low-grade inflammatory condition expressed by inflammation and immune damage that mediates component(s) of insulin resistance and cardiometabolic syndrome in the presence of disruption of circadian rhythms. Primary research data indicate that the interplay between biological timing and immunological signalling occurs in a synchronised manner to govern metabolic homeostasis, thereby leading us to coin the term Circadian regulation of metabolic inflammation. These signalling pathways directly affect immune cell trafficking and endothelial integrity in sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1PR1) or purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7)-mediated regulation, and inflammasome activation. This review highlights a new molecular link establishing the S1PR1-P2X7 axis between circadian rhythm and obesity-linked immunometabolic disorders. We discuss the interplay of lipid and purinergic signalling, focusing on their convergence at nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/Akt), signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), reactive oxygen species (ROS), and NOD-, LRR-, and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) activation pathways that act in concert to exacerbate both fatty tissue inflammation and systemic insulin metabolic resistance. Altogether, we summarise the latest advances in receptor-based pharmacotherapy, chronotherapy, and nanomedicine-guided drug delivery aimed at restoring circadian homeostasis and metabolic balance. Understanding the circadian regulation of the S1PR1-P2X7 axis may inform new precision treatment strategies for obesity-linked metabolic diseases.

papers.title: Sleep Spindles and Slow Oscillations as Potential Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets in Mild-to-Moderate Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.abstract: This review critically evaluates evidence on sleep spindles (SP), slow oscillations (SOs), and their coordination in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD), focusing on their relationships with cognition, AD biomarkers, and their therapeutic potential. Longitudinal studies associate greater SP and/or SO activity with better cognition and favourable amyloid and tau profiles after clinical onset. Spindle and SO coupling may index network integrity. Preserved NREM sleep oscillations are associated with lower orexin concentrations and weaker adverse relationships between orexin and cognitive and neuropsychiatric outcomes. Closed-loop acoustic stimulation and slow-oscillatory transcranial direct-current stimulation can modify SO activity, spindle activity, and coupling, although cognitive and biomarker benefits remain uncertain. Spindle-SO activity, including their temporal coupling, are associated with cognition and AD biomarkers across the disease continuum. Closed-loop acoustic and electrical stimulation can modify these oscillations, but biomarker-characterized trials in MCI and AD are needed to determine whether treatment produces durable cognitive and biomarker benefits.

papers.title: Effects of resistance training on subjective sleep quality, excessive daytime sleepiness, and quality of life in patients with obstructive sleep apnea: a secondary analysis from a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to verify the effect of eight weeks of resistance training (RT) on subjective sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and quality of life in adults with OSA. In this randomized controlled clinical trial, 25 adults with moderate to severe OSA (age: 54.6 ± 7.2 years; BMI: 36.1 ± 7.9 kg/m²; apnea-hypopnea index: 52.2 ± 27.4 events/hour) were included. Participants were randomized into an RT group (three sessions per week) or a control group [CG (two sessions per week)]. Sleep quality, excessive daytime sleepiness, and quality of life were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), SF-36, respectively. Generalized estimated equations verified differences between groups over time. Differences were observed in domains sleep latency (RT: Δ -1.0 ± 0.3 vs. CG: 0.2 ± 0.2; p = 0.018), sleep duration (RT: Δ -0.6 ± 0.3 vs. CG: -0.2 ± 0.2; p = 0.012), sleeping medication (RT: Δ -0.2 ± 0.1 vs. CG: 0.8 ± 0.3; p = 0.007), and overall PSQI score (RT: Δ -3.2 ± 0.6 vs. CG: 0.2 ± 0.8; p = 0.004). Regarding SF-36, differences were found in emotional aspects (RT: Δ 29.6 ± 14.8 vs. CG: -17.9 ± 10.0; p = 0.008) and global score (RT: Δ 10.8 ± 3.3 vs. CG: -3.4 ± 3.1; p = 0.002) were observed. No difference was observed in ESS. An eight-week RT program improves subjective sleep quality and quality of life in adults with moderate to severe OSA. Clinical trial registration (Brazilian Clinical Trials Registry [ReBec]): # RBR-2rg97kz. Date of registration: 01/17/2025.

papers.title: Sleep, Dietary Intake, and Physical Activity: Examining Bidirectionality Using Repeated-Measures Analyses.
papers.abstract: Studies examining how sleep impacts diet and activity and vice versa have been limited by the use of aggregate data in cross-sectional designs. We examined how sleep might influence diet and physical activity the next day, and daytime diet and activity relate to sleep that night, using temporal repeated-measures analyses. Twenty-four-hour time use (sleep onset, wake after sleep onset, total sleep time, sedentary time, light physical activity [LPA], and moderate-vigorous physical activity [MVPA]) was measured (AX3 accelerometers) over 7 days in adolescents (11-14.9 years) in Dunedin, New Zealand (March-December 2021). Bedtime was reported in daily diaries. Multiple-pass 24-hour dietary recalls were collected on days 3, 5, and 7. Mixed-effects regression models were used with participants as a random effect, adjusted for weekend days. In 75 youth (mean age 12.9 y, 36% indigenous Māori, 37.3% overweight or obese), going to bed 1 hour later was associated with less LPA (mean difference; 95% confidence interval: -3.8 minutes; -6.1 to -1.6) and MVPA (-14.0 minutes; -22.6 to -5.3) the next day. By contrast, LPA and MVPA during the day were not related to sleep that night. On days when bedtime was later, youth were more sedentary (25 minutes; 11-39, for each hour later) and consumed significantly more energy from ultraprocessed (618 kJ; 248-988) and noncore (732 kJ; 350-1113) foods and less from core foods (-419 kJ; -781 to -57). Sleep timing appears more strongly related to diet and physical activity than total sleep time in youth. Encouraging earlier bedtimes might be a practical target to reduce obesity risk.

papers.title: Long-Term Outcome Following Idiopathic Ventricular Fibrillation and Potential Emerging Etiologies.
papers.abstract: Unexplained cardiac death and cardiac arrest associated with idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (IVF) are heterogeneous pathologies responsible for significant mortality in young people. This retrospective multicenter cohort study evaluated the natural history of a large cohort of IVF survivors including recurrence burden, emerging etiologies, and long-term management. This study included IVF patients from 46 tertiary centers and followed for at least 5 years. Patients over the age of 15 years who had documented ventricular fibrillation and extensive negative investigations supporting the diagnosis of IVF were included. Patients were followed in each center with their outcome being established on data collection from subsequent clinical records, new investigations, genetic results, and implanted defibrillator recordings. Recurrent arrhythmias and mortality were assessed. Diagnoses were graded as definite (direct evidence) or probable (indirect criteria). A total of 825 patients (37% women; age 35.7 ± 12 years) were followed for a median duration of 120 months (Q1-Q3: 78-180 months). Death occurred in 27 patients (3.3%) from cardiac (n = 10; 1.2%), noncardiac (n = 9; 1.1%), and unknown (n = 8; 1%) causes, and few patients (4.5%) developed overt cardiomyopathy. Overall arrhythmia recurrence increased steadily over 2 decades, reaching 52.7% of patients, with a median time to first recurrence of 20 months (Q1-Q3: 5-48 months) and a similar incidence in men and women. Emergent etiologies occurred in 68.8% of the total population, and were associated with new information during recurrences, structural changes, genetic results, and mapping procedures. They included reclassified inherited arrhythmia conditions in 73 (8.8%), focal sources in 272 (33.0%), and definite or probable microstructural myocardial alterations (MiCMs) with normal imaging in 223 (27.0%), while no diagnosis was identified in 257 (31.2%). Compared with MiCM, focal IVF included more women, occurred more frequently at rest/sleep, and was associated with narrow QRS complexes (90.1 ± 12 milliseconds vs 104.8 ± 16 milliseconds; P < 0.001). Quinidine appeared effective in preventing focal IVF (68.3%) whereas beta-blockers appeared effective (49.3%) in MiCM-IVF. Catheter ablation was performed in 181 patients with no recurrence observed in 75.7%. This multicenter long-term cohort study of IVF survivors shows low cardiac mortality, a persistent risk of arrhythmia recurrences over time, and identifies potential emerging etiologies.

papers.title: [Spectral-topographic features of EEG in patients with varying rates of alcohol dependence progression].
papers.abstract: To compare the spectral-topographic characteristics of the background electroencephalogram (EEG) in patients with alcohol dependence, differing in disease progression rate, as part of a pilot study. A total of 40 male patients with a confirmed diagnosis of alcohol dependence (F10.2 according to ICD-10) were examined. Utilizing a retrospective evaluation of the development of alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS), participants were classified into two distinct groups: those exhibiting rapid progression (≤3 years, n=23) and those with slow progression (≥12 years, n=17). Background EEG recordings were obtained using a 16-channel system (10-20 configuration), followed by spectral analysis of absolute power in the theta, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 frequency bands. The analysis revealed that patients with rapid progression demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in the spectral power of the alpha-1 rhythm across all cortical regions (p<0.002 after correction), with the most pronounced effects observed in frontal and central leads. There were also reductions noted in the power of alpha-2, theta (except the parietal region), and beta-1 (limited to the frontal area) frequency bands. Notably, 74% of patients with rapid progression exhibited a low-amplitude («flattened») EEG pattern, whereas 71% in the slow progression group maintained a normal alpha rhythm. The results indicate the presence of a distinct neurophysiological endophenotype associated with the rapid progression of alcohol dependence. Key characteristics of this endophenotype include a overall decrease in the power of the alpha-1 rhythm, particularly in the front-central leads; a decline in theta power (excluding the parietal region); a frontal-specific reduction in beta-1 power; and a significant prevalence of low-amplitude EEG patterns.

papers.title: [The correlation of interleukin 2 and interleukin 4 with alterations in the brachiocephalic arteries in patients with obstructive sleep apnea].
papers.abstract: To evaluate the relationship between interleukin 2 (IL-2) and interleukin 4 (IL-4) and the alterations occurring in the extracranial levels of arteries of patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). A total of 65 subjects participated in the study, comprising 40 males (61.5%) and 25 females (38.5%), with a mean age of 52.86±9.75 years. The subjects were categorized into two distinct groups: the main group, consisting of 37 patients with OSA and an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of more than 15 episodes per hour, and the control group, consisting of 28 subjects without OSA and an AHI of less than 5 episodes per hour. The diagnostic procedure for all subjects encompassed anthropometric measurements, polysomnography, and ultrasound imaging of the brachiocephalic arteries (BCA). The assessment of chronic cerebral ischemia (CCI) and hypertension (HTN) was conducted. IL-2 and IL-4 levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Among patients diagnosed with OSA, CCI was detected in 75.7% of cases, and atherosclerotic changes in the BCA were observed in 89.2%. Furthermore, these patients presented with a bilateral increase in the diameters of the common carotid artery (CCA) and the internal carotid artery (ICA) (p<0.05), alongside a noted increase in IL-2 levels and a significantly reduced IL-4 levels. In the main group, a positive correlation was established between the diameter of the left ICA and IL-4 (r=0.421, p=0.009), as well as between the diameter of the right ICA and IL-4 (r=0.482, p=0.003). A positive association was also observed between the detected atherosclerotic alterations and neck circumference (r=0.269, p=0.030), AHI (r=0.255, p=0.041), HTN (r=0.336, p=0.006), and CCI (r=0.255, p=0.041). The findings of this study demonstrate that patients with OSA exhibit increasingly persistent and significant abnormalities in the extracranial arteries as the pathological process advances. The noted dilation of the ICA and the CCA in the main group is likely due to vascular remodeling and reduced IL-4 levels. The established correlation between atherosclerotic changes in the BCA and metrics such as neck circumference, AHI, HTN, and CCI suggests that OSA may directly induce pathological processes in vascular walls, thereby contributing to the emergence of comorbid conditions. The absence of a definitive link between BCA atherosclerosis and IL-4 levels in OSA patients may be attributable to the relatively small sample size, warranting further research.

papers.title: [Experience in the implementation of a comprehensive non-pharmacological therapeutic program at the Center for Cognitive and Psycho-Emotional Health].
papers.abstract: To analyze the outcomes of a complex non-pharmacological treatment regimen administered to patients at the daytime hospital (DH) of the Center for Cognitive and Psycho-Emotional Health (CCPH) and to evaluate the changes in the cognitive and psycho-emotional state of the patients. The study included 103 patients attending the CCPH DH, with a mean age of 46.98±14.32 years; 76.7% were female. Participants were categorized into three distinct groups: Group 1 with predominantly cognitive impairments (CIs), Group 2 with predominantly psycho-emotional disorders, and Group 3 with sleep disorders. Cognitive and psycho-emotional statuses were assessed using widely accepted tests and assessment scales. Each participant underwent a tailored five-day course of non-pharmacological therapy, which integrated cognitive training, biofeedback-based electroencephalography training, physical therapy, and neurostimulation techniques. Treatment outcomes were assessed after the intervention. Following the therapeutic intervention, 91.26% of participants demonstrated clinical improvement, with the greatest improvement observed in Group 2 (96.6%). No deterioration in clinical status was noted among any of the patients, thereby affirming the safety of the therapeutic interventions. Neuropsychological test results indicated a statistically significant improvement across all three groups (p<0.05), reflected in enhanced cognitive metrics and a reduction in anxiety and depressive symptoms among patients with pre-dementia CIs, anxiety disorders, and chronic insomnia. While a tendency towards improvement was noted in patients with severe ICs, the changes did not reach statistical significance, particularly in patients with isolated depressive disorders, potentially due to the limited sample size. Moreover, patients within Group 3 showed improvements in sleep during the therapy. The findings suggest that a five-day non-pharmacological intervention with an integrated approach represents an effective and safe method for the maintenance and enhancement of cognitive and psycho-emotional health.

papers.title: [Neurocognitive characteristics in children with sluggish cognitive tempo].
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the neurocognitive characteristics of children diagnosed with sluggish cognitive tempo (SCT) and to evaluate the efficacy of Cortexin in addressing this condition. The main study group included 40 children aged 12 to 14 years with symptoms consistent with SCT manifestations. The comparison group consisted of 30 children with combined ADHD (ADHD-C), also aged 12 to 14 years. The control group comprised 30 children in the same age range without any neuropsychiatric disorders. The study used several methods, including S. Lee's SCT scale for assessing the severity of SCT symptoms, the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI-20), the Daytime Sleepiness Scale, and T.A. Fotekova and T.V. Akhutina's reading skills assessment method, the «Working Memory» method to quantifying working memory capabilities, the TOVA computer test, and EEG (routine and spectral analysis). Cortexin was administered intramuscularly at a standard dosage of 10 mg every other day across 10 injections to patients diagnosed with SCT. The study results showed that children with SCT, in comparison to their counterparts with ADHD-C and healthy peers, exhibited significantly more pronounced asthenic symptoms and a higher prevalence of comorbid learning disorders. Quantitative EEG analysis revealed a reduced theta-to-alpha wave power ratio in the anterior cerebral cortex of the SCT group compared with the ADHD cohort. These findings support the hypothesis that children with SCT are less prone to exhibiting deficits in inhibition processes, while instead demonstrating a decline in overall levels of functional activity maintenance. A follow-up assessment after treatment revealed improvements in inattention, severity of working memory impairment, asthenic symptoms, and reading skills in 82% of cases. Additionally, EEG analysis post-treatment indicated a reduction in alpha-band power in the frontal and central leads of both hemispheres, suggesting enhanced overall cortical activation. This study has delineated several cognitive characteristics associated with SCT in children and demonstrated that administering Cortexin significantly alleviates the primary symptoms of SCT and mitigates the manifestation of major comorbid disorders.

papers.title: [Mild cognitive impairment as a heterogeneous condition: From diagnostic algorithm - to individualized therapeutic approaches].
papers.abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is a prevalent syndrome affecting approximately 10-15% of the global population. In the Russian Federation, the estimated number of individuals with MCI may reach 5 million, with continued growth projected. Subjective cognitive deficits are linked to an increased risk of dementia, although memory complaints are often regarded as a normal aspect of aging. Standard neuropsychological assessments, including the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Mini-Cog, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), often lack sufficient sensitivity to detect MCI, particularly in individuals with high cognitive reserve. MCI has multiple etiologies, including depression and other affective disorders, severe somatic diseases, traumatic or toxic brain injury, and neurodegenerative or vascular pathologies of the central nervous system. This etiological diversity leads to variable clinical outcomes: cognitive function may return to age-appropriate norms in some instances, while in others, early impairment progresses to dementia. High-risk factors for conversion from MCI to dementia include the amnestic subtype of cognitive impairment, slow gait, coexisting affective disorders, sensory deficits, senile preasthenia and asthenia, and sleep disturbances. Accurate prediction of disease progression is critical for informing therapeutic strategies. For patients at elevated risk of progression, pharmacological interventions should be selected not only for symptomatic management but also for their potential to delay conversion. In Russia, Miladean, a combination of memantine and melatonin, is approved for use in patients with MCI. In addition to its symptomatic benefits, Miladean exhibits neuroprotective and endothelioprotective properties, supporting its use as the preferred treatment for patients at high risk of MCI progression.

papers.title: Intracranial lymphatic dysfunction after traumatic brain injury: Imaging biomarkers, neural repair, and non-invasive modulation.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury initiates secondary processes that may persist long after the initial mechanical insult. These processes may be amplified when tissue fluid, cellular debris, inflammatory mediators, metabolites, and abnormal proteins accumulate faster than the brain can redistribute or eliminate them. The relevant clearance apparatus is a serial-parallel network comprising cerebrospinal fluid-interstitial fluid exchange, perivascular transport, brain-meningeal interfaces, meningeal lymphatic vessels, and cranial, spinal, and cervical outflow pathways. Traumatic brain injury may disrupt this network through altered aquaporin-4 polarization, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, edema, pressure abnormalities, disturbed sleep and autonomic regulation, and neuroinflammation. This dysfunction does not necessarily represent a uniform reduction in flow; rather, it may involve phase- and phenotype-specific transport bottlenecks. This review integrates these mechanisms within an injury-clearance-repair framework, evaluates available imaging biomarkers, and classifies therapeutic evidence according to the directness of transport-target engagement. Current evidence remains predominantly preclinical, and most non-invasive interventions require mechanistic validation specifically in traumatic brain injury. Translation will depend on compartment-specific biomarkers, phase-appropriate safety assessments, and the establishment of a causal link between transport correction, neural repair biology, and functional recovery. The therapeutic objective is not the indiscriminate enhancement of "flow," but the restoration of coordinated transport across the rate-limiting step that constrains recovery.

papers.title: Lifestyle factors associated with hot flash frequency and daily interference: highlighting the role of sleep quality, diet quality and physical activity.
papers.abstract: To examine associations of lifestyle and demographic factors with hot flash frequency (HFF) and hot flash-related daily interference (HFRDI) in a multicultural Australian convenience sample. The study fills an evidence gap by investigating how lifestyle factors interact with ethnicity and self-reported menopausal status in Australia's diverse population, an area with limited prior research. A cross-sectional online survey conducted in 2024-2025 included a convenience sample of women who self-identified as being in perimenopause and postmenopause (mean age: 56.1±6.6 y). All demographic, menopause, lifestyle, medication-use, and symptom information was self-reported through the online questionnaire. Demographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, menopause status, and symptom outcomes were self-reported. Diet quality, physical activity, and sleep were assessed using an adapted Global Diet Quality Score, an International Physical Activity Questionnaire-based measure, and a modified Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, respectively. Menopause status was self-reported, and duration in that status was recorded; Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop (STRAW) +10 informed the terminology but was not used to assign specific reproductive-aging substages. Outcomes included HFF and HFRDI. Ordinal logistic models estimated adjusted associations controlling for age, menopause status/duration, and ethnicity. Sleep quality was the strongest correlate of HFF and HFRDI. For HFF, each one-category worsening in sleep quality was associated with higher odds of being in a higher frequency category (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]=2.44; P=0.001); older age was inversely associated (aOR=0.42; P=0.002). For HFRDI, poorer sleep was strongly associated with greater interference (aOR=4.93; P<0.001). Ethnicity was not associated with frequency (P=0.687) but was associated with daily interference (aOR=2.66; P=0.037). Diet quality showed a nonsignificant inverse association for daily interference (P=0.077). Physical activity showed a small, nonsignificant tendency toward higher frequency (P=0.135). Findings suggest the importance of routine sleep quality for symptom burden and may inform lifestyle-focused approaches to symptom management.

papers.title: Adolescent Chronic Sleep Restriction Induces a Mesolimbic Hypodopaminergic State Associated with Addiction Vulnerability.
papers.abstract: Adolescent sleep insufficiency is increasingly prevalent, but whether repeated insufficient sleep during this developmental period promotes addiction vulnerability remains unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of chronic sleep restriction (CSR) imposed during adolescence, from 4 to 7 weeks of age, on the mesocorticolimbic dopamine (DA) system and addiction-related behaviors in mice. Behavioral and neuronal responses in the mesolimbic pathway to the psychostimulant Amphetamine (Amph) were examined. Also, DA-related molecular and structural components, including DA receptors, DA turnover, and developmental regulators such as Netrin-1/deleted in colorectal cancer (DCC), were assessed. Our results identified that adolescent CSR induces a hypodopaminergic profile characterized by reduced neuronal activity in the core regions of the mesolimbic DA circuit at baseline and upon acute Amph stimulation, downregulated striatal DA receptors, and reduced DA axon innervation in the ventral striatum. Altered Netrin-1/DCC signaling and mesocortical DA synthesis further suggest that sleep loss during adolescence disrupts ongoing maturation of DA circuitry. Furthermore, these neurobiological profiles were accompanied by enhanced Amph-induced conditioned place preference (CPP). Together, these findings indicate that chronic adolescent sleep insufficiency induces a constellation of behavioral and neurobiological adaptations relevant to addiction susceptibility. In contrast to prior acute sleep-loss paradigms that mainly capture transient DA activation, our data support a model in which repeated sleep restriction imposes cumulative allostatic load and promotes longer-term maladaptive remodeling of reward circuitry. These results identify insufficient sleep during adolescence as a potential risk factor for addiction vulnerability.

papers.title: The network localization and underlying biological basis of heterogeneous structural and functional brain abnormalities in insomnia disorder.
papers.abstract: Insomnia disorder (ID) has become a prevalent sleep disorder worldwide, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear due to heterogeneous neuroimaging findings and uncertain network localization. We identified brain structural and functional abnormality locations associated with ID from 63 published neuroimaging studies, including 3391 patients and 3433 healthy controls. Using coordinate network mapping combined with a normative connectome database, we mapped these abnormalities to large-scale brain networks of ID across imaging modalities and further decoded them by integrating microscale chemo-architectural, cellular, and cognitive maps. The structural network widely involved the ventral attention (VAN), sensorimotor (SMN), dorsal attention (DAN) and default mode network (DMN); the task-induced network showed a similar but less extensive pattern, predominantly implicating the VAN, DMN, SMN and subcortical network (SCN); in contrast, the resting-state network was largely confined to the left middle frontal gyrus and the bilateral mid-cingulate cortex. Molecular mapping revealed both shared and distinct neurotransmitter signatures across the three networks, involving cholinergic, histaminergic, glutamatergic, noradrenergic, and opioid systems. Cellular decoding showed relatively selective associations of the structural and task-based networks with glial cells and excitatory neurons, whereas the resting-state network exhibited broader associations with glial cells and multiple excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes. Cognitive decoding linked structural and task-based networks to sensorimotor processing and the resting-state network to memory-related functions. Our findings reconcile heterogeneous neuroimaging results and reveal neurobiological substrates of ID from a network perspective, providing a promising biomarker and paving the way for circuit-based precision therapies of ID.

papers.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding.
papers.abstract: Objective. Speech Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question.Approach. Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG.Main results. We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. In contrast, there are significant overlaps in signal timings contributing to EEG-based decoding, regardless of vocal conditions such as overt or covert speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions.Significance. Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.&#xD.

papers.title: Overnight changes in exhaled carbon dioxide, oxygen, and nitrous oxide in obstructive sleep apnea: associations with disease severity and polysomnographic findings.
papers.abstract: Exhaled breath analysis is a non-invasive approach for assessing physiological alterations in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This study evaluated overnight changes in exhaled CO₂, O₂, and N₂O concentrations and their associations with OSA severity and polysomnographic parameters.Methods: In this prospective observational study, 62 adults undergoing diagnostic overnight polysomnography were enrolled and classified as having no OSA (n = 21), mild-to-moderate OSA (n = 21), or severe OSA (n = 20) according to the apnea-hypopnea index. Exhaled CO₂, O₂, and N₂O concentrations were measured immediately before and after overnight polysomnography under standardized conditions.Results: Morning exhaled N₂O concentrations were significantly higher in patients with severe OSA than in the other groups (p = 0.001). Overnight changes in exhaled CO₂ (ΔCO₂), N₂O (ΔN₂O), and O₂ (ΔO₂) differed significantly according to OSA severity (all p < 0.001). Compared with the no OSA group, patients with OSA exhibited greater overnight increases in exhaled CO₂ and N₂O concentrations together with greater decreases in exhaled O₂ concentrations. Overnight ΔN₂O and ΔO₂ showed strong correlations with AHI (ρ = -0.760 and 0.912, respectively; both p < 0.001) and ODI (ρ = -0.713 and 0.913, respectively; both p < 0.001).Conclusion: Patients with OSA exhibited more pronounced overnight alterations in exhaled gas composition, particularly greater changes in exhaled O₂ and N₂O concentrations. These findings suggest that dynamic overnight exhaled gas changes may reflect physiological alterations associated with OSA severity and warrant further validation in larger prospective studies.&#xD.

papers.title: ADHDeepNet: An Explainable Framework for EEG-Based ADHD Detection From Raw Signals.
papers.abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common brain disorder in children that can persist into adulthood, affecting social, academic, and career life. Early diagnosis is crucial for managing these impacts on patients and the healthcare system but is often labor-intensive and time-consuming. This paper presents a novel method to improve ADHD diagnosis precision and timeliness by leveraging Deep Learning (DL) approaches and electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. We introduce ADHDeepNet, a deep learning model that utilizes comprehensive temporal-spatial characterization, attention modules, and explainability techniques optimized for EEG signals. ADHDeepNet integrates feature extraction and refinement processes to enhance ADHD diagnosis. The model was trained and validated on a dataset of 121 participants (61 ADHD, 60 Healthy Controls), employing nested cross-validation for robust performance. The proposed two-stage methodology uses a 10-fold cross-subject validation strategy. Initially, each iteration optimizes the model's hyper-parameters with inner 2-fold cross-validation. Then, Additive Gaussian Noise (AGN) with various standard deviations and magnification levels is applied for data augmentation. ADHDeepNet achieved 100% sensitivity and 99.17% accuracy in classifying ADHD/HC subjects. To clarify model explainability and identify key brain regions and frequency bands for ADHD diagnosis, we analyzed the learned weights and activation patterns of the model's primary layers. Additionally, t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) visualized high-dimensional data, aiding in interpreting the model's decisions. This study highlights the potential of deep learning and EEG in enhancing ADHD diagnosis accuracy and efficiency.

papers.title: Sleep Duration and Mental Well-Being Among Older Chinese Adults: A Four-Wave Fixed-Effects Analysis Using CHARLS.
papers.abstract: To examine within-person associations between nighttime sleep duration and mental well-being among older Chinese adults. We analyzed four waves of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS; 2011-2018) using individual fixed-effects linear regressions with wave fixed effects and individual-clustered standard errors. Outcomes were CES-D-10 depressive symptoms and reverse-coded life satisfaction. Sleep was modeled continuously and categorically, with main categories of ≤6 h, >6 to <9 h, and ≥9 h; sensitivity models used ≤ 5 h, >5 to <9 h, and ≥9 h. Among observations with valid CES-D-10 data, 36.74% met the ≥10 screening threshold. Each additional hour of sleep was associated with lower CES-D-10 scores (β = -0.305) and higher life satisfaction (β = 0.015). Compared with the main reference range, short sleep was associated with higher CES-D-10 scores (β = 0.846) and lower life satisfaction (β = -0.046). Long-sleep estimates varied by specification and outcome. Shorter nighttime sleep duration, particularly sleep in the operational short-sleep category, was associated with poorer mental well-being within individuals over time. Usual sleep duration can inform mood and sleep assessment but should not substitute for evaluation of sleep quality or sleep disorders.

papers.title: Understanding Chrononutrition for Managing Shift Workers' Health: A Narrative Review and Future Directions.
papers.abstract: Shift workers have temporal eating patterns characterised by irregular food intake and prolonged periods of eating with more energy intake occurring in night-time hours during night shifts. These patterns of eating against a backdrop of shift work exacerbate circadian misalignment, which impairs cardiometabolic profiles and increases the risk of developing overweight and obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. Limiting food intake at night and being mindful about food choices is beneficial on night shifts, but further research is required to determine appropriate timing and composition of food intake. Some food intake at night may be necessary in supporting individual alertness and performance at work and should be considered when recommending that shift workers minimise food intake at night. At the individual level, shift workers may benefit from minimising night-time food intake during night shifts. At the organisational level, healthy food consumption habits should be encouraged by improving access to healthy food at night, implementing scheduled meal breaks and providing information about healthy eating guidelines to employees. Medical professionals and Accredited Practising Dietitians (APD) should be aware of the impact of circadian misalignment on metabolic health and consider this when educating patients on adhering to healthy eating guidelines.

papers.title: Glycemic Indices and Polysomnographic Parameters in an Iranian Population Referred to a Sleep Clinic.
papers.abstract: Diabetes remains a significant global health burden, with sleep breathing disorders increasingly implicated in its development and progression. In this study, we aimed to assess the relationship between glycemic indices and polysomnography (PSG) parameters among patients referred to a sleep clinic in Iran. We retrospectively studied adults at the Baharloo Hospital sleep clinic who completed overnight PSG and a recent metabolic panel, as well as validated questionnaires on sleepiness, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) risk, and insomnia, between March 2024 and March 2025. We examined associations using Pearson correlations and adjusted linear regression models. A total of 409 participants (115 females) were included. Correlation analyses revealed that higher HbA1c and fasting blood glucose (FBS) were associated with worse nocturnal oxygenation profiles, with HbA1c showing a more selective pattern. Moreover, after adjusting for confounding factors, higher HbA1c was independently associated with lower mean nocturnal oxygen saturation (beta = -0.159, p = 0.013) and lower non-REM oxygen saturation (beta = -0.179, p = 0.007). Meanwhile, higher FBS was independently associated with lower average oxygen saturation during wake (beta = -0.688, p = 0.018) and during REM sleep (beta = -0.890, p = 0.001). Our study highlights the relationship between glycemic measures and sleep parameters in a relatively large population of Iranian sleep clinic patients. More studies are needed to unravel the association between diabetes and sleep breathing disorders to identify their shared mechanisms.

papers.title: Interventions to Address Sleep Disparities in the United States: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: The purpose of this narrative review is to synthesize existing literature on interventions that address sleep disparities across the lifespan. These populations include racial and ethnic minoritized populations, individuals with disabilities, sexual and gender minoritized communities, socioeconomically disadvantaged individuals, and those living in both rural and urban environments. We identified 16 studies focused on interventions targeting sleep disparities among racial and ethnic minoritized, socioeconomically disadvantaged, rural, and urban populations. Key intervention strategies included culturally, racially, linguistically, and individually tailored messaging; remote and community-based delivery to increase access; and stress management techniques. Despite evidence of sleep disparities, there is a lack of research focused on interventions targeting these disparities, especially among individuals with disabilities and sexual and gender minoritized communities. This narrative review highlights the need for culturally relevant, accessible, and scalable solutions across all populations who experience sleep disparities.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbances in Chronic Kidney Disease - The CKD-REIN Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Insomnia and excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) are common in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), but their determinants are poorly understood. We analyzed multiple factors likely to affect sleep with the aim of disentangling the contributions of CKD markers and symptoms from those of social factors, lifestyle, comorbid conditions, and drug-induced effects, with the latter 2 highly prevalent in this population. Prospective cohort study. In total, 2,765 patients with CKD stages 2-5 not receiving dialysis (mean age, 67 ± 13 years; 66% men) from a representative sample of 40 nephrology clinics in France. Albuminuria, estimated glomerular filtration rate, CKD symptoms, lifestyle, comorbid conditions, and medications collected annually. Insomnia and EDS ≥ 3 times/week in the past 3 months assessed with a standardized questionnaire at baseline, 1-, 3-, and 5-year follow-ups, providing 7,264 observations overall. Adjusted odds ratios of insomnia and EDS associated with time-updated exposures estimated with mixed effects logistic regressions. Baseline prevalence of reported insomnia was 22% (95% confidence interval, 21%-24%) and that of EDS, 15% (14%-16%). Based on the 7,264 observations, neither prevalence was associated with albuminuria after adjustment for age and gender. The odds ratio of EDS alone increased significantly with decreasing estimated glomerular filtration rate, 1.16 (1.05-1.28 mL/min/1.73 m2) per 10 mL/min/1.73 m2, independent of social factors, physical activity, obesity, heart failure, and long half-life benzodiazepine use. It was no longer significant after adjustment for fatigue, which displayed a strong dose-effect relation with EDS, depression, insomnia, and sleep apnea. Insomnia prevalence increased strongly with severity of cramps, itching, and stress, independent of other determinants including female gender, heart failure, thyroid hormone use, depression, and sleep apnea. Self-reported sleep disturbances and limited longitudinal inference. This study highlights the multifactorial nature of sleep disturbances in CKD and the potentially modifiable contribution of CKD symptoms and drug-induced effects.

papers.title: Glucocorticoids in breast cancer: physiologic mechanisms and relationship to risk, survival, and treatment response.
papers.abstract: Almost every cell of the body expresses glucocorticoid receptors (GR). Cell density, isoform distribution, and responsiveness vary greatly among tissues with highest density in cells of the immune system. Well-documented basic studies describe functions of GR-cortisol complex in immune cells; inhibition of inflammation, promotion of apoptosis, inhibition of proliferation, and inhibition of transport into tissues. Basic studies also describe metabolic actions; promotion of gluconeogenesis, amino acid mobilization, impairment of insulin secretion, inhibition of glucose uptake, and expansion of visceral fat depots. Cortisol secretion is stimulated by psychological stress, and by physiological responses to pain, infection, and hypoglycemia. Stimulatory inputs from the brain on CRH and AVP biosynthesis, deficiencies in the negative feedback of cortisol, and insufficient stimulation of β-arrestin-1 by cortisol may all act to increase secretion of ACTH. Peripherally, cortisol activity is preserved by 11βHSD type I and is decreased at specific sites by 11βHSD type 2. In metastatic breast cancer, the normal circadian rhythm of serum and salivary cortisol is often disrupted, with great hour-to-hour variation and elevated concentrations during the afternoon nadir. Cortisol may increase cancer risk by making glucose available through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, by inhibiting insulin promotion of glucose uptake, and by inhibiting IGF-I promotion of leukocytopoiesis, increasing the synthesis of glutamine synthetase, inhibiting ICAM-I and VCAM-1 for leukocyte recruitment, and increasing the expression of immune checkpoint receptors PD-1 and Tim3, and increasing Treg cells. Cortisol promotes the polarization of macrophages toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype and decreases the M1 phenotype. It also binds to membrane-bound corticosteroid-binding globulin, activating adenylyl cyclase, suppressing T cell proliferation. Overall, elevated cortisol secretion may promote growth of breast cancer by providing a substrate for growth and by suppression of host defenses. However, by antagonizing the estrogen response the liganded receptor may inhibit the growth of estrogen-dependent breast cancer. This review is relevant at this time because of the many interactions of glucocorticoids with potential treatments for the several subtypes of breast cancer. Glucocorticoid agonists may benefit therapies utilizing DNA damage response, retinoid therapy, and PARP1 therapy but may oppose therapies of ER-negative cancers and immune checkpoint blockade therapy.

papers.title: Latent Profiles of Psychological Distress and Suicidal Ideation Among Nursing Students: A Cross-Sectional Study of Associated Factors.
papers.abstract: Psychological distress and suicidal ideation frequently co-occur among nursing students, but their heterogeneity is often overlooked. To identify latent profiles of nursing students based on psychological distress and suicidal ideation dimensions, and to explore factors associated with profile membership. A cross-sectional survey of 1461 Chinese nursing students was conducted. Latent profile analysis (LPA) was applied to psychological distress and suicidal ideation dimensions to identify profiles, and multinomial logistic regression was used to examine factors associated with profile membership. Three latent profiles emerged: C1: Low distress-low suicidal ideation (60.4%), C2: moderate distress-moderate suicidal ideation (30.8%), and C3: high distress-high suicidal ideation (8.8%). Multinomial regression revealed factors associated with C2/C3 vs. C1, including poor sleep quality, internet overuse/addiction, and moderate self-efficacy. Factors associated with lower likelihood of C2 vs. C1 included good academic performance, moderate/high self-esteem, and moderate/high time management skills. Factors associated with higher likelihood of C3 vs. C1 included higher body mass index (BMI), undergraduate institution enrollment, morning/neutral chronotypes, whereas exercise ≥1 time/week and a good parental relationship were associated with lower likelihood of C3 vs. C1. Nursing students exhibit three profiles, with 8.8% belonging to C3. Profile-informed screening and preventive strategies considering factors associated with profile membership (sleep quality, internet addiction, exercise frequency, time management, self-esteem, and self-efficacy) and contextual stressors (institution type, BMI, and parental relationship) may inform future screening approaches for students exhibiting elevated psychological distress and suicidal ideation patterns.

papers.title: Unraveling the Genotype-Phenotype Landscape of Kleefstra Syndrome Through EHMT1 Variant Analysis.
papers.abstract: Kleefstra syndrome type 1 (KLEFS1) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EHMT1, which play a key role in epigenetic regulation. Core features include global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects (CHDs), and neuropsychiatric manifestations. This retrospective study included patients with KLEFS1 evaluated at Seoul National University Hospital between January 2022 and April 2025. Genetic diagnoses were made using chromosomal microarray or whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To enhance statistical power, we conducted a joint analysis with established cohorts of at least 30 clinically characterized patients. Among the 15 patients with KLEFS1, 14 (93.3%) exhibited GDD or ID, with frequent comorbidities such as CHDs (8/12, 66.7%), orthopaedic manifestations (6/12, 50.0%), epilepsy (6/15, 40.0%), and sleep problems (4/11, 36.4%). Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in 10 of the 12 patients (83.3%), including pituitary anomalies in 2 (16.7%). By combining our data with recently published multicenter international cohorts, we assessed genotype-phenotype correlations by comparing the clinical features of 202 patients with different variant subtypes. Patients with multigene deletions had a significantly higher prevalence of CHDs (53.5% vs 25.8%, p value = 2 × 10-4), cortical visual impairment (12.5% vs 1.7%, p value = 0.004), microcephaly (37.1% vs 17.8%, p value = 0.009), corpus callosum abnormalities (17.9% vs 5.9%, p value = 0.02), and hearing impairment (39.7% vs 25.6%, p value = 0.04) than those with single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) or short insertions/deletions (indels), in addition to the previously identified features including epilepsy, constipation, and short stature. We also observed that a recurrent EHMT1 variant (p.Arg948Trp), identified in multiple unrelated patients, was linked to significant phenotypic heterogeneity, including late-onset neurocognitive regression. Our study showed that patients with multigene deletions are significantly more likely to exhibit multiorgan involvement, including CHDs, cortical visual impairments, microcephaly, corpus callosum abnormalities, and hearing impairments, compared with those with SNVs or indels, emphasizing the importance of genotype-informed management. We report pituitary gland abnormalities in KLEFS1, expanding the phenotypic and neuroimaging spectrum of KLEFS1. The patient showing regression in their 30s necessitates long-term, comprehensive studies to support care.

papers.title: Clinically suspected central nervous system Richter transformation presenting with progressive psychiatric symptoms: A case report.
papers.abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) involvement associated with Richter transformation (RT) is a rare complication of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Neurological manifestations are heterogeneous. To our knowledge, no previous reports have described CNS RT presenting predominantly with psychiatric and behavioral symptoms. We report a clinically suspected case of CNS RT presenting predominantly with progressive psychiatric symptoms in the presence of extensive CNS lesions but without apparent focal neurological deficits. A 71-year-old man with no psychiatric history developed progressive personality change, irritability, emotional lability, behavioral disinhibition, and sleep-wake cycle disturbance. Gadolinium-enhanced fluid-attenuated inversion recovery magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated newly developed multifocal lesions predominantly involving the bilateral temporal lobes. Hematological evaluation established previously unrecognized CLL. Although histopathological confirmation was not obtained, the overall clinical, radiological, and laboratory findings supported CNS involvement associated with clinically suspected RT as the most likely diagnosis. Progressive neuropsychiatric deterioration limited invasive diagnostic procedures and disease-directed treatment. Supportive and palliative management was provided, and the patient died of aspiration pneumonia 114 days after surgery. This case demonstrates that clinically suspected CNS RT may present predominantly with progressive psychiatric and behavioral symptoms in the absence of focal neurological deficits. Severe neuropsychiatric symptoms may themselves impede diagnostic confirmation and disease-directed treatment. When pathological confirmation is not feasible, multidisciplinary discussion and shared decision-making with the patient and family, together with explicit acknowledgment of diagnostic uncertainty and careful balancing of the benefits and burdens of further investigation and treatment, may support patient-centered care.
papers.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences

papers.title: Diffusion tensor MR neurography reveals altered sciatic and tibial nerve microstructure in chronic dialysis patients.
papers.abstract: Uremic polyneuropathy is a complication of chronic kidney disease, presenting as a distal symmetric neuropathy mainly attributed to axonal damage. Electrophysiology provides limited insight into microstructural nerve alterations. Magnetic resonance neurography (MRN) may enable assessment of peripheral nerve integrity. This study aimed to quantify sciatic and tibial nerve microstructural changes in chronic dialysis patients and evaluate their clinical relevance. Thirty patients on chronic dialysis (DP)-without prediabetes or diabetes-and 30 healthy controls (HCs) underwent MRN, including diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). All MRN datasets of the distal thigh (30/30) were suitable for analysis. Four lower-leg examinations in the patient cohort (26/30) and three in the healthy group (27/30) were excluded because of motion artifacts. Fractional anisotropy (FA) was defined as the primary imaging outcome, while axial diffusivity (AD) and radial diffusivity (RD) were analyzed as secondary metrics. Electrophysiological testing was not available in four patients in the dialysis cohort (26/30). Results were compared between groups and correlated with electrophysiological, clinical, and laboratory findings. FA of the sciatic (DP 0.44, HC 0.48, P < .001) and tibial nerve (DP 0.38, HC 0.43, P < .0001) and AD were significantly reduced in dialysis patients, while RD did not differ between groups. Lower FA correlated with electrophysiological measures, neuropathy scores, and was independently associated with group after adjustment for age, BMI, and sex. Subgroup analyses showed lower FA in patients fulfilling electrophysiological criteria for uremic polyneuropathy but no difference according to dialysis modality. The reduction in FA and AD, together with electrophysiological and clinical correlations, is compatible with a predominantly axonal pattern of peripheral nerve involvement in chronic dialysis patients. DTI detected peripheral nerve microstructural alterations associated with chronic dialysis. These findings support further longitudinal and disease control studies to determine the clinical utility of DTI as an imaging biomarker in chronic dialysis patients.

papers.title: Effect of Long-Term Physical Exercise on Memory, Anxiety-Like Behavior, and Depression in Young and Aged Male Mice Subjected to Sleep Deprivation.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether chronic aerobic exercise could attenuate behavioral impairments associated with sleep deprivation (SD) in young and aged male mice. Young (3 months) and aged (18 months) Swiss mice were assigned to four groups: control, exercise (EXE), sleep deprivation (SD), and exercise followed by SD (EXE + SD). Animals performed treadmill training for 8 weeks and then underwent 72-hour SD. Behavioral tests assessed working memory (Y-maze), depression-like behavior (tail suspension), and anxiety-like behavior (elevated plus maze). The results suggest that age influences the effectiveness of exercise in mitigating sleep deprivation-induced behavioral deficits, opening avenues for future studies on the interaction between physical exercise, sleep, and aging.

papers.title: Pulsed Field Ablation for Cardiac Arrhythmias: Industry Landscape and US Food and Drug Administration-approved Platforms (2025).
papers.abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has rapidly advanced from an experimental modality to a front-line therapy for catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation (AF). Unlike thermal approaches such as radiofrequency (RF) or cryoablation, PFA relies on irreversible electroporation, producing rapid and selective myocardial lesions with minimal risk of collateral injury. This review examines the contemporary landscape of PFA technology, with emphasis on recent United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approvals that have expanded PFA from single-energy, single-shot systems toward focal and hybrid ablation strategies. Particular focus is placed on FDA-approved platforms, including PulseSelect™ (Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA), FARAPULSE™ (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA), and VARIPULSE™ (Biosense Webster, Diamond Bar, CA, USA), as well as next-generation systems such as the Affera Sphere-9™ dual-energy RF-PFA platform (Medtronic) and the Volt™ focal PFA system (Abbott, Chicago, IL, USA). Differences in catheter design, energy delivery, workflow, mapping integration, regulatory labeling, and clinical outcomes are reviewed. By contextualizing these platforms within evolving ablation strategies, this review highlights a second evolutionary phase of PFA focused on procedural flexibility, lesion durability, and integration with established electrophysiology (EP) workflows, with implications for future AF management and EP lab practice.
